sections.h2: How does an Ohio foreclosure end in a sheriff sale?
sections.html:
A lender files a foreclosure suit in the county court of common pleas, wins a judgment, and the court orders the property sold. R.C. 2323.07 says the court may order a tract sold whole or in parcels, and where land lies in several counties it may direct the sheriff of each county or one officer to sell it. The sale itself is then run under Chapter 2329.

The Supreme Court of Ohio's foreclosure mediation guide warns that once a borrower receives notice of the lawsuit, the home could be lost in three to six months. It advises opening every piece of mail from the court, contacting the servicer right away, and staying in the house. Occupancy is advised because the home stays in better condition and the lender prefers it that way until the sheriff says otherwise.

Hotlines listed on the Ohio Attorney General's foreclosure page include Save the Dream Ohio at 888-404-4674, the Ohio Department of Commerce at 800-750-0750, Ohio State Legal Services Association at 866-529-6446 and HUD approved counselors at 888-995-HOPE.

sections.h2: How is an Ohio house appraised before the sheriff sells it?
sections.html:
The sheriff calls three disinterested freeholders, who must live in the county and own real property there, to appraise the land on actual view. Under R.C. 2329.17, for a residence they have twenty-one calendar days from the clerk's order to return a value. If they miss that window, the freeholders are not paid, the appraised value becomes the auditor's most recent value, and the sale moves ahead. A court can approve a separate appraisal for good cause.

The same section lets the municipality or township inspect any structures on the land before the sale. Ask the sheriff's office whether an inspection has been scheduled for your property.

The appraisal sets the floor for the first auction. Under R.C. 2329.20, land may not be sold for less than two-thirds of its appraised value, with exceptions in sections 2329.51 and 2329.52. A junior lien holder enforcing against land subject to a prior lien faces a modified minimum figure, set by the court.

sections.h2: What notice does an Ohio sheriff sale require?
sections.html:
Two kinds of notice are needed. R.C. 2329.26 requires the creditor or its attorney to serve a written notice on the judgment debtor and each other party, and to file that notice with proof of service at least seven calendar days before the sale. A party in default for failing to appear in the case does not have to be served. The officer must also advertise the sale once a week for at least three consecutive weeks in a newspaper of general circulation in the county.

The advertisement states the date, time and place, or for an online sale the start date, minimum duration and web address. It also states the required deposit and tells bidders they answer for costs, allowances and taxes the proceeds do not cover.

These rules have teeth. Under R.C. 2329.27, a sale made without the required notices is set aside on motion of an interested party. Once the court confirms a sale, though, that order is treated as a finding that notice was adequate and bars further motions to set the sale aside. A homeowner who spots a notice defect needs to raise it before confirmation.

sections.h2: What are the deposit and second auction rules?
sections.html:
A bidder other than the foreclosing lender must put down a deposit set by the home's appraised value. R.C. 2329.211 sets three tiers for residential property:

  • Two thousand dollars when the appraisal is ten thousand dollars or less.
  • Five thousand dollars when the appraisal is above ten thousand and up to two hundred thousand.
  • Ten thousand dollars when the appraisal is above two hundred thousand.

A purchaser who misses the deposit timing makes the sale invalid, and the home can go to a provisional second sale if one was announced.

If a house in a residential mortgage foreclosure fails to sell at the first auction, R.C. 2329.52 calls for a second auction between seven and thirty days later. That auction goes to the highest bidder with no minimum bid, though costs, allowances and real estate taxes still have to be covered. A house still unsold after two auctions may be offered again without the minimum or disposed of in another way allowed by the chapter.

sections.h2: What are the steps from judgment to deed, and what do they say?
sections.html:
The table lays out the statutory sequence a homeowner can watch on the court docket.

sections.h2: Can I redeem or stop an Ohio sheriff sale?
sections.html:
Yes, until the court confirms the sale. R.C. 2329.33 lets the debtor deposit with the clerk the judgment amount, all costs, and interest at eight percent a year on the purchase money from the day of sale. The court then sets the sale aside, applies the deposit to the judgment and awards the interest to the bidder. After confirmation, redemption under that section is gone.

Timing is tight. R.C. 2329.31 says the court reviews the sale and journalizes confirmation within thirty days of the return of the writ, though it may stay confirmation to let an owner redeem. The buyer then has thirty days after confirmation to pay the balance, and the officer records the deed within fourteen days after confirmation and payment. If the deed is late, the buyer can ask for a court order that works as the deed. The county auditor then updates ownership for tax purposes, and taxes coming due after the sale fall on the new owner.

A sale of the house itself can produce the redemption money. Ask the plaintiff's attorney for a written payoff, check the docket with the clerk, and keep the confirmation date in view.

Mediation is another route. The Supreme Court's guide says a foreclosure case can be mediated from before filing up to confirmation of the sale, and that even after the sheriff sale it has been done. Programs vary by county court, so call the court. After a sale, the guide describes the general order of payment as the court, the sheriff, the county treasurer, then lien holders, with any remainder going to the owner. The guide also warns that some firms charge fees for services that are available for free, and that Save the Dream Ohio referrals cost nothing.

faqs.q: How long does a sheriff sale take after a foreclosure judgment in Ohio?
faqs.a: The statutes set pieces, not one total. Appraisal takes up to twenty-one days, advertising runs at least three weeks, confirmation follows within thirty days of the writ's return, and the buyer has thirty days to pay. Ask the clerk for the dates on your case.

faqs.q: What is the minimum bid at an Ohio sheriff sale?
faqs.a: Two-thirds of the appraised value at the first auction. For a residential mortgage foreclosure, a second auction held seven to thirty days later has no minimum bid. Costs and real estate taxes still have to be covered.

faqs.q: Can I redeem my Ohio home after the sheriff sale?
faqs.a: Only before the court confirms the sale. You deposit the judgment amount, costs and eight percent interest on the purchase money with the clerk. Once confirmed, that right ends.

faqs.q: Do I have to move out before the Ohio sheriff sale?
faqs.a: No. The Supreme Court of Ohio's guide urges owners to stay in the home and keep it in good condition until the sheriff says they must leave.

faqs.q: Where can I get free help with an Ohio foreclosure?
faqs.a: Call Save the Dream Ohio at 888-404-4674, or the Ohio State Legal Services Association at 866-529-6446. HUD approved counselors are at 888-995-HOPE. Your county common pleas court can tell you whether it offers foreclosure mediation.
